items.prose: A candle burns down at a steady rate. Two hours after it is lit it is 21 cm tall, and five hours after it is 13.5 cm. Plot time $t$ in hours across and height $h$ in cm up.

parts.question: What is the gradient of the line through $(2, 21)$ and $(5, 13.5)$, in cm per hour? Give a decimal.

feedback.generic: Not quite. Divide the change in height by the change in time, keeping the sign.

byKey.sign: The candle gets shorter, so the line falls: the rise is $13.5 - 21 = -7.5$, and $m = -2.5$.
byKey.flipped: You divided the run by the rise. The gradient is rise over run: $-7.5 \div 3$.
byKey.no-run: $-7.5$ cm is the fall over 3 hours. Divide by the 3: $-2.5$ cm per hour.

explain.text: The rise is $13.5 - 21 = -7.5$ cm and the run is $5 - 2 = 3$ hours. So $m = -7.5 \div 3 = -2.5$: the candle loses 2.5 cm each hour.

parts.question: Using the gradient $-2.5$, how tall was the candle when it was lit, at $t = 0$? Give a whole number of cm.

feedback.generic: Not quite. Put the point $(2, 21)$ into $h = -2.5t + c$ and solve for $c$.

byKey.sign: You took 5 off. Going back 2 hours the candle was taller: $21 + 2.5 \times 2 = 26$.
byKey.first-point: 21 cm is the height at $t = 2$, not at $t = 0$. Go back two hours: $21 + 5 = 26$.
byKey.one-hour: You went back one hour. The point is at $t = 2$, so go back two: $21 + 2 \times 2.5 = 26$.

explain.text: At $t = 2$ the height is 21, so $21 = -2.5 \times 2 + c = -5 + c$. That gives $c = 26$: the line is $h = 26 - 2.5t$.

parts.question: Using $h = 26 - 2.5t$, after how many hours does the candle burn out? Give a decimal.

feedback.generic: Not quite. Burnt out means $h = 0$. Solve $26 - 2.5t = 0$.

byKey.sixteen: That follows from a start of 16 cm. With $c = 26$: $26 \div 2.5 = 10.4$ hours.
byKey.times: You multiplied, $26 \times 2.5$. Each hour takes 2.5 cm, so 26 cm last $26 \div 2.5$ hours.
byKey.flipped: You divided 2.5 by 26. The hours are the height over the cm lost each hour: $26 \div 2.5$.

explain.text: Set $h = 0$: $26 - 2.5t = 0$, so $t = 26 \div 2.5 = 10.4$ hours. That is 10 hours and 24 minutes.

parts.question: Using the burn-out time of 10.4 hours, where does the line meet the horizontal axis?

options.why: The time goes across, so it is the first coordinate. $(0, 10.4)$ is on the vertical axis.
That is where the line meets the vertical axis, when the candle is lit.
26 is a height in cm, not a time. The time across at burn-out is 10.4.

feedback.correct: On the horizontal axis the height is 0, and that happens at $t = 10.4$. So the point is $(10.4, 0)$.
feedback.generic: Not quite. A point on the horizontal axis has height 0. Write the time first.

explain.text: A point is written $(t, h)$: across first, then up. At burn-out $h = 0$ and $t = 10.4$, so the line meets the horizontal axis at $(10.4, 0)$.

items.prose: On a park plan, in units of 10 m, a straight path runs through $A(-2, 1)$ and $B(5, 29)$. A pipe will run from a drain at $D(12, 23)$ to the path, meeting it at a right angle.

parts.question: What is the gradient of the path? Give a decimal if it is not whole.

feedback.generic: Not quite. Divide the rise from A to B by the run from A to B.

byKey.flipped: You divided the run by the rise. The gradient is rise over run: $28 \div 7$.
byKey.lost-minus: You took the run as $5 - 2$. It is $5 - (-2) = 7$, so $m = 28 \div 7$.

explain.text: From A to B the rise is $29 - 1 = 28$ and the run is $5 - (-2) = 7$. So $m = 28 \div 7 = 4$.

parts.question: Using the gradient 4, complete the path's equation $y = \ldots$. Type only what comes after the $=$ sign.

feedback.generic: Not quite. Put $A(-2, 1)$ into $y = 4x + c$ and solve for $c$.

byKey.c-first: 1 is the height of A, at $x = -2$. The intercept is the height at $x = 0$: $1 + 4 \times 2 = 9$.
byKey.sign: You added $4 \times (-2) = -8$ to 1 instead of taking it off. $1 = -8 + c$ gives $c = 9$.
byKey.flipped: That uses the gradient 0.25. The path climbs 28 over a run of 7, so $m = 4$.

explain.text: A is on the path, so $1 = 4 \times (-2) + c = -8 + c$ and $c = 9$. Check B: $4 \times 5 + 9 = 29$.

parts.question: Using the path's gradient 4, what gradient must the pipe have? Give a decimal.

feedback.generic: Not quite. The two gradients must multiply to $-1$.

byKey.reciprocal: You flipped 4 but kept the sign. $0.25 \times 4 = 1$, not $-1$, so the pipe needs $-0.25$.
byKey.negative: You changed the sign but did not flip. $-4 \times 4 = -16$, not $-1$.
byKey.same: A shared gradient makes the lines parallel. A right angle needs $m_1 \times m_2 = -1$.

explain.text: For a right angle $m_1 \times m_2 = -1$. With $m_1 = 4$, $m_2 = -1 \div 4 = -0.25$, the negative reciprocal.

parts.question: The pipe has gradient $-0.25$ and passes through $D(12, 23)$. Complete its equation $y = \ldots$. Type only what comes after the $=$ sign.

feedback.generic: Not quite. Put $D(12, 23)$ into $y = -0.25x + c$ and solve for $c$.

byKey.c-first: 23 is the height of D, at $x = 12$. Solve $23 = -0.25 \times 12 + c$, so $c = 26$.
byKey.sign: You added $-3$ instead of taking it off. $23 = -3 + c$ gives $c = 26$.
byKey.reciprocal: That uses the gradient 0.25, which is not perpendicular to 4. The pipe has gradient $-0.25$.

explain.text: D is on the pipe, so $23 = -0.25 \times 12 + c = -3 + c$ and $c = 26$. Check: $-0.25 \times 12 + 26 = 23$.

parts.question: Using $y = 4x + 9$ and $y = -0.25x + 26$, at what $x$ does the pipe meet the path? Give a decimal if it is not whole.

feedback.generic: Not quite. Set the two right-hand sides equal and collect the $x$ terms on one side.

byKey.y-value: 25 is the $y$-coordinate of the meeting point $(4, 25)$. The question asks for $x$.
byKey.sign-x: You took $0.25x$ from $4x$ instead of adding it. Moving $-0.25x$ across gives $4.25x = 17$.
byKey.constants: You added the 9 to the 26. Moving $+9$ across takes it off: $4.25x = 26 - 9 = 17$.

explain.text: Where the lines meet they have the same $y$, so $4x + 9 = -0.25x + 26$. Add $0.25x$ and take off 9: $4.25x = 17$, so $x = 4$. Then $y = 25$, and the pipe meets the path at $(4, 25)$.

items.prose: Gym A charges a £20 joining fee and £24 a month. Gym B charges a joining fee and a fixed monthly amount too. Its statements show £104 paid in all after 3 months and £194 after 8 months.

parts.question: Gym B's total cost line passes through $(3, 104)$ and $(8, 194)$. What is its monthly charge, in pounds? Give a whole number.

feedback.generic: Not quite. Divide the change in cost by the change in months.

byKey.no-run: £90 is the cost of 5 months. Divide by the 5: £18 a month.
byKey.one-point: You divided one total by its months, $104 \div 3$. That total holds the joining fee too.

explain.text: From month 3 to month 8 the total rises £90 over 5 months. So the gradient is $90 \div 5 = 18$ pounds a month.

parts.question: Using £18 a month, what is Gym B's joining fee, in pounds? Give a whole number.

feedback.generic: Not quite. Put $(3, 104)$ into $y = 18x + c$ and solve for $c$.

byKey.first-point: £104 is the total after 3 months. Take off the 3 monthly charges: $104 - 54 = 50$.
byKey.sign: You added the £54. It is part of the £104, so take it off: $104 - 54 = 50$.
byKey.no-run: That uses £90 a month, the cost of 5 months. With £18: $104 - 54 = 50$.

explain.text: The intercept is the cost at 0 months, the joining fee. From $(3, 104)$: $104 = 18 \times 3 + c$, so $c = 50$. Check: $18 \times 8 + 50 = 194$.

parts.question: Gym A costs $y = 24x + 20$ and Gym B $y = 18x + 50$ after $x$ months. After how many months have they cost the same? Give a whole number.

feedback.generic: Not quite. Set the two costs equal, then collect the $x$ terms on one side.

byKey.fee-gap: £30 is the gap in the joining fees. Gym A closes it at £6 a month: $30 \div 6 = 5$.
byKey.fees-sum: You added the 20 instead of taking it off, so $6x = 70$. Take 20 from both sides: $6x = 30$.

explain.text: The lines meet where the costs are equal: $24x + 20 = 18x + 50$. Take $18x$ and 20 from both sides: $6x = 30$, so $x = 5$. Both cost £140 then.

parts.question: The lines cross at 5 months, and after that Gym B is cheaper. How much cheaper is Gym B over 12 months, in pounds? Give a whole number.

feedback.generic: Not quite. Work out each total for 12 months, then take one from the other.

byKey.rates-only: £72 is the gap in monthly charges over 12 months. Gym B also charged £30 more to join: $72 - 30 = 42$.
byKey.gym-b: £266 is what Gym B costs over 12 months. The question asks how much less than Gym A.
byKey.gym-a: £308 is what Gym A costs over 12 months. Take Gym B's £266 from it.

explain.text: Put $x = 12$ into each line: £308 for A and £266 for B. Gym B is £42 cheaper. That is 7 months past the crossing at £6 a month.

items.prose: Asha opens a savings jar with £40 and adds £15 every week. Ben's jar, which also grows in a straight line, holds £50 after 2 weeks and £110 after 6 weeks.

parts.question: Asha's savings after $x$ weeks are $y = 15x + 40$. Fill in her table of values: how much is in her jar after 6 weeks, in pounds? Give a whole number.

feedback.generic: Not quite. Multiply the weeks by 15, then add the £40 she started with.

byKey.no-start: £90 is what she added in 6 weeks. She started with £40: $90 + 40 = 130$.
byKey.swapped: You used £40 a week and a £15 start. She starts with £40 and adds £15 a week.

explain.text: Six weeks of £15 is £90. With the £40 she started with, the jar holds £130, the point $(6, 130)$.

parts.question: Ben's points are $(2, 50)$ and $(6, 110)$. How much does Ben add each week, in pounds? Give a whole number.

feedback.generic: Not quite. Divide the change in savings by the change in weeks.

byKey.no-run: £60 is what Ben adds over 4 weeks. Divide by the 4: £15 a week.
byKey.one-point: You divided one total by its weeks, $50 \div 2$. Ben did not start at £0.

explain.text: From week 2 to week 6 Ben's jar rises £60 over 4 weeks. So he adds $60 \div 4 = 15$ pounds a week.

parts.question: Using £15 a week, how much did Ben start with, in pounds? Give a whole number.

feedback.generic: Not quite. Put $(2, 50)$ into $y = 15x + c$ and solve for $c$.

byKey.first-point: £50 is what Ben had after 2 weeks. Take off the 2 weeks of £15: $50 - 30 = 20$.
byKey.sign: You added the £30. It is part of the £50, so take it off: $50 - 30 = 20$.
byKey.one-point: That follows from £25 a week. With £15 a week: $50 - 30 = 20$.

explain.text: The intercept is the amount at week 0. From $(2, 50)$: $50 = 15 \times 2 + c$, so $c = 20$. Ben's line is $y = 15x + 20$.

parts.question: Part 1 put Asha at £130 after 6 weeks, when Ben has £110. Asha's line is $y = 15x + 40$ and, from part 3, Ben's is $y = 15x + 20$. When does Ben's jar catch up with Asha's?

options.text: Never: the two lines are parallel
After 20 weeks, since the gap is £20
options.why: The gap is £20, but it never shrinks: both add £15 a week.
The $15x$ terms cancel and leave $40 = 20$, which is never true.
That would need Ben to add more each week than Asha. Both add £15.

feedback.correct: Both lines have gradient 15, so they are parallel and never meet. Ben stays £20 behind every week.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Compare the gradients of the two lines first.

explain.text: Lines with the same gradient keep the same gap and never meet. Here both gradients are 15 and the intercepts are 40 and 20. So the gap stays at £20 for ever.
